clinicalPearls: Slow-flow malformation present at birth as a flat, sharply demarcated pink to red patch that grows proportionately with the child and does not involute.
Caused by somatic activating mutations in GNAQ (and related genes such as GNA11), the same pathway implicated in Sturge-Weber syndrome.
Facial lesions in the frontal or ophthalmic (V1) distribution carry a risk of Sturge-Weber syndrome with leptomeningeal and ocular involvement.
Tends to darken, thicken and develop nodular cobblestoning with age.
Overgrowth of underlying soft tissue and bone can occur, especially with segmental facial or limb lesions.
Pulsed dye laser is the treatment of choice for cosmetically significant lesions and is most effective when started early.
Distinguish from the common, transient naevus simplex (salmon patch or stork bite), which usually fades in infancy.
A geographic, well-demarcated capillary stain on a limb may signal an overgrowth syndrome such as capillary malformation-arteriovenous malformation (RASA1) or a PIK3CA-related overgrowth disorder.
reference.pathophysiology: Capillary malformation is a congenital slow-flow malformation of dermal capillaries and postcapillary venules arising from somatic mosaic activating mutations, most commonly in GNAQ, which constitutively activate Galpha-q signalling through the MAPK/ERK pathway in endothelial cells. This causes progressive ectasia of superficial dermal vessels and deficient perivascular neural regulation. Unlike vascular tumours there is no endothelial proliferation; the vessels are structurally abnormal and dilate over time, accounting for progressive darkening and thickening of the lesion.
additionalDifferentials: Macular precursor of an early infantile haemangioma
Capillary malformation of an overgrowth syndrome (Klippel-Trenaunay, CLOVES, Sturge-Weber)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis, with dermoscopy as an adjunct
Contrast-enhanced brain MRI when Sturge-Weber syndrome is suspected (V1 distribution)
Ophthalmology review with intraocular pressure measurement for at-risk facial lesions
Limb imaging and length assessment where overgrowth is suspected
Genetic testing (GNAQ, RASA1, PIK3CA) in syndromic presentations
redFlags: V1 or forehead facial distribution with seizures or developmental concern (Sturge-Weber syndrome)
Warmth, thrill or bruit suggesting a high-flow arteriovenous malformation
reference.prognosis: A capillary malformation is a lifelong lesion that tends to darken and thicken with age. Laser therapy lightens most lesions, and the wider prognosis depends on any associated syndromic features.
pitfalls: Confusing a persistent port-wine stain with a self-resolving salmon patch.
Failing to screen V1-distribution facial lesions for Sturge-Weber syndrome and glaucoma.
Overlooking a limb overgrowth syndrome behind an apparently simple capillary stain.
Missing an evolving arteriovenous malformation masquerading as a capillary stain.
references: Reviews of capillary malformations and Sturge-Weber syndrome genetics
management: Pulsed dye laser as the treatment of choice for cosmetically significant lesions, most effective when started early
Contrast-enhanced brain MRI and ophthalmology review for high-risk facial (V1) lesions to detect Sturge-Weber syndrome
Ophthalmic surveillance with intraocular pressure monitoring for glaucoma in at-risk facial lesions
Monitoring for soft-tissue and bony overgrowth in segmental facial or limb lesions, with limb-length assessment
Psychological support and camouflage cosmetics for visible lesions
Referral to a vascular anomalies multidisciplinary team for syndromic or extensive disease
Genetic evaluation in syndromic presentations, recognising the underlying somatic mosaic GNAQ mutation
